title: Verifiable quantum advantage in extremely low depth
abstract: We give a sampling problem that is solvable by shallow quantum circuits, hard for polynomial-time classical algorithms under lattice-based assumptions, and efficiently verifiable by a classical computer. The quantum sampler admits two implementations: one uses log-logarithmic-depth quantum circuits with one- and two-qubit gates, i.e., $\mathsf{QNC}^0[\log\log]$ circuits, while the other uses constant-depth quantum circuits with unbounded fan-in gates, i.e., $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits. Our construction can be seen as compiling the Learning with Errors (LWE)-based single-round proof of quantumness of Arabadjieva et al. (2025) to very low depth. The price paid for this compilation is the reliance on less standard, though well-motivated, assumptions: in addition to the lattice knowledge assumption used by Arabadjieva et al. (2025), we require a strengthened variant of the adaptive-hardcore-bit property of LWE, for which we provide supporting evidence. Unlike previous low-depth proofs of quantumness, the quantum computation here requires no mid-circuit measurements or feed-forward: it consists only of running a shallow circuit and sampling from its output distribution. This shows that shallow quantum circuits have sufficient structure to solve certain classically hard tasks whose solutions can be verified efficiently.
summary: This paper constructs a sampling problem that proves quantum advantage using quantum circuits with remarkably low depth ($\log \log \lambda$ or constant). It achieves this by adapting existing lattice-based proofs of quantumness, requiring only shallow circuit execution and sampling, which is a significant step toward practical quantum cryptography demonstrations.
main_problem: To construct a sampling problem that is solvable by extremely shallow quantum circuits, computationally hard for classical algorithms based on lattice assumptions, and efficiently verifiable.
main_result: The authors provide constructions showing that quantum advantage can be demonstrated using circuits of depth $O(\log \log \lambda)$ or even constant depth ($QAC^0$), without requiring mid-circuit measurements.
method: The work compiles existing lattice-based proofs of quantumness (like those from Arabadjieva et al.) into low-depth quantum circuits, framing the problem as a challenge-response protocol.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum circuits operating on qubits, specifically analyzing the capabilities of shallow circuits defined by $QNC^0[\log \log]$ or $QAC^0$ gate sets. The underlying hardness relies on the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem.
key_observables: Acceptance probability of the quantum sampler, the depth of the required quantum circuit, and the computational advantage over classical samplers.
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($\log \log \lambda$ or constant), security parameter ($\lambda$), and the lattice knowledge assumption strength ($	ext{LK-}1/4$).
main_assumptions: The construction relies on non-standard assumptions, including a strengthened variant of the adaptive-hardcore-bit property of LWE and the $	ext{LK-}1/4$ assumption.
figures_summary: The notes refer to a table comparing various quantum advantage protocols based on depth, measurements, and fan-out/fan-in, indicating the current work improves these metrics.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon previous work (BCMVV, AGGM) by focusing on reducing the circuit depth. It establishes the necessary quantum sampling problem and proves the existence of polynomial-size quantum circuits achieving the desired low depth while maintaining classical hardness.
why_interesting: This work pushes the boundary of quantum complexity theory by demonstrating that quantum advantage can be shown using extremely shallow circuits, which is highly relevant for near-term quantum hardware feasibility.
